question: Using the customary setting of the mathematics used for quantum mechanics, is it possible to prove the existence of Gödelßs god-like entities?

2.text:
In the mathematical metalanguage that is used to set up quantum mechanics you can
formalise Gödel's modal ontological argument at all.

The customary mathematics of non-relativistic quantum mechanics is the
classical set theory ZFC together with the theory of separable complex
Hilbert spaces, self-adjoint operators, spectral measures, etc.  First
order modal logic S5 is a conservative extension of first order logic and
hence interpretable in ZFC.  Once the language of properties is given a
formal domain and the five Gödel axioms

* $P(x)\rightarrow \Box P(x)$,
* $P(x)\rightarrow P(\exists yR(y,x))$,
* etc.

for the predicate $P$ of “positive property’’ are adopted, Gödel’s
derivation

$ \Diamond \exists x G(x) \rightarrow \Box \exists x G(x)$

with

$G(x)\equiv \forall P\,[P(x)\to P(x)]$, 

is a theorem of S5.  In particular the derivation is a theorem of the
classical mathematics in which a Hilbert space $H$, the algebra
${\cal B}(H)$, etc., is defined.  Formally that is all there is to say:
the proof is a purely syntactic theorem of the classical meta-theory
used to speak about $H$.  It is conditional on the substantive
metaphysical axioms about positivity and about the modal principles of
S5 and it does not give an empirical or physical existence claim.  In
that sense the argument lives in the same classical metalanguage that
underlies the textbook Hilbert-space formalism.

If the proof is wanted to live inside the quantum-theoretic notion of
property and truth, i.e. inside the orthomodular quantum logic that is
naturally associated with the lattice $L(H)$ of closed subspaces of a
Hilbert space, then the situation changes.  The Gödelian maximal being
is the entity that possesses every positive property essentially and at
the same time in every possible world.  That requires a global,
non-contextual bivalent valuation of the whole lattice of properties.
Kochen–Specker contextuality and the failure of distributivity in
$L(H)$ is exactly the statement that the usual Hilbert-space
formalism does not admit such a simultaneous definite truth-value
assignment to all observables/properties.  Hence the simultaneous
maximal conjunction of positive properties that the ontological proof
needs has no quantum-logical realisation.  In the physically operative
reading of the Hilbert-space formalism the proof is therefore empty:
the formalism supplies the classical metalanguage in which the modal
derivation can be written down, but it supplies no quantum-mechanical
reason to accept the positivity axioms or the required non-contextual
maximal valuation.  That is the usual reason for saying the argument
is formal and not a physical proof of existence.

7.text:
In the physics literature the “mathematics of quantum mechanics’’ is the
ordinary classical mathematics in which the physical formalism is written
down, i.e.  ZFC set theory with the analysis that goes with complex separable
Hilbert spaces, C*-algebras, spectral theory etc. That background is
more than strong enough to formalise modal predicate logic and therefore
to formalise Gödel’s ontological argument exactly as it is formalised in
the logic literature.

What can be written down is the usual S5 formalisation

G1  P x → P □x
G2  P x → P(¬x → y)
G3  P x → P( x → y) → P y
G4  P x → P(x ∨ y)  etc.

together with

Ess x := ∀P [P x → P x] ,   God x := ∀P [P x ↔ P x] ,
and the definitions of positive, necessarily positive, essentially … 
and the axiom  P x → P □x and the axiom “Existence is positive’’,
P∃.  In the classical metatheory that underlies the Hilbert space
formalism this is a perfectly ordinary first order, indeed set theoretic,
theory.  If the usual S5 axioms and the positivity axioms are accepted
the theorem

⊢ □∃x God x

is a theorem of that metatheory.  In that completely formal sense the
proof can be carried out in the same ZF + analysis in which
H^∞ ,  L(H), the spectral theorem, the Schrödinger equation etc. are
written.

The point is that nothing in the Hilbert space calculus, in the
operator algebra, in the Born rule or in any of the usual quantum
computations ever produces the modal notions □,◊, the predicate
“positive property’’ or the axiom that existence is a positive property.
The ontological argument is a theorem of modal logic with a very
special non-empirical axiom set.  It is not a consequence of the
equations of quantum mechanics and it does not make any empirical
prediction about Hilbert space.  In the strict physical sense the
formalism contains no modal operators at all and hence no necessity
assertion about a God-like being can be derived from the physical
formalism itself.  The existence claim is a purely formal-logical
consequence of the Gödel axioms in the classical background
mathematics that the physicist uses, and it remains a metaphysical
premise-laden result rather than a physical theorem of quantum theory.

5.text:
The Hilbert space / C* algebra formalism that is ordinarily used for
quantum mechanics is just ordinary classical mathematics. Up to
interpretation it is ZFC plus real and complex analysis, linear
algebra and spectral theory. That is the background in which the
Hilbert space of states, self-adjoint operators as observables and the
Born rule are defined.

Gödel’s ontological argument is not a theorem of analysis on a
Hilbert space. It is a theorem of first order modal logic S5 with a
substantive, essentially metaphysical, theory of properties. In the
usual rendering one has

* P(x): x is a positive property;
* P(x) → □ P(x);
* P(x) ∧ P(y) → P(x ∧ y);
* P(x) → P(□∃x)

and the Definition

* G(x) := ∀P [ P(x) → P(x) ] i.e. x has all positive properties,

together with the modal axiom

* □∃x G(x) → ∃x G(x)

and the axiom that necessary existence is positive.
From these premises S5 proves

* ∃x G(x)

and indeed □∃x G(x). 

That is a purely logical-metaphysical derivation. It can of course be
written down in the set-theoretic language which also underlies the
mathematics of quantum mechanics, so in the trivial syntactic sense it
is formalizable in the same first-order background. It is not however
a consequence of the physical postulates of quantum mechanics and it
does not become a physical theorem by being written in the same
background set theory.

In the genuine quantum logical reading the situation is even worse.
The lattice of propositions of an ordinary quantum system is the
orthomodular lattice of closed subspaces of a Hilbert space. It is
non-distributive and the classical Boolean laws on which the usual
treatment of positivity, conjunction and negation in Gödel’s proof
rest are not valid. The distributive inferences that are used to pass
from P and ¬P to a contradiction are exactly what fails in quantum
logic. Hence the S5 argument does not transfer to the non-classical
propositional calculus that is the natural logic of the customary
quantum-mechanical formalism.

So as a physical consequence of quantum mechanics there is nothing to
prove. The existence of a Gödelian god-like, necessarily existent
being with all positive properties is a modal-metaphysical claim whose
premises are not theorems of the Hilbert-space formalism, and which
in fact ceases to be a valid derivation once the formalism is read in
the quantum logical sense in which the usual distributive laws fail.
That is the usual way of saying that one cannot prove the existence
of a metaphysical entity from the mathematics of physics.

1.text:
In the physics the mathematics which is actually used is not new mathematics.
The non relativistic formalism is a theory of complex separable Hilbert
spaces, self adjoint operators and spectral measures. The whole of that
can be, and in the physics literature is, formalised in ZFC + ordinary
analysis. It is first order set theory with the usual analytic apparatus.

Gödel's ontological argument is a modal first order argument in the
language $L_{prop}$ with a unary modal operator $\Box$ and the predicate
$P(x)$ ' $x$ is a positive property'.  With the usual Gödel axioms

* $P(x)\rightarrow \Box P(x)$,
* $P(x)\rightarrow P(\neg x)$ is false,
* $G(x)\equiv \forall P\,[P(x)\rightarrow P(x)]$ is positive,
* etc.,

one obtains in the normal modal logic S5

$\Box \exists x G(x)$

and hence $\exists x G(x)$.  That is a theorem of S5 + the axiom
scheme $\{A_{i}\}$ about positivity.

Formalisation of $L_{prop}$ and of S5 is completely ordinary: properties
can be coded by subsets of the domain, $\Box$ can be interpreted in any
normal Kripke frame, and the whole calculus is a fragment of ZFC.  In
that purely syntactic sense the argument can be written down inside the
set theory which underlies the functional analysis of quantum theory.

What is not inside the Hilbert space formalism are the $A_{i}$.  The
axioms that

* being positive is closed under entailment,
* God-like $G(x)\equiv\forall P[P(x)\to P(x)]$ is positive,
* necessarily existent properties are positive,

are substantial metaphysical principles about the essence of
positivity and of necessity.  They are not consequences of the
axioms of a complex Hilbert space, of the spectral theorem, of the
Born rule or of any empirical content of quantum mechanics, and they are
independent of ZFC.  Hence the customary mathematical setting of
quantum mechanics gives you a place to formalise the proof, but it does
not give you the premises.  The existence of a Gödelian God like entity
is provable only conditionally on the acceptance of Gödel's modal
metaphysics, and that conditional proof is not a theorem of the
physical mathematics of QM alone. ∎

3.text:
In the ordinary way QM is done the formalism lives in the ordinary
classical set theory / analysis which is used for Hilbert spaces,
bounded operators on a complex separable Hilbert space, spectral theory,
C*-algebras etc.  Modal Propositional Calculus S5 and, a fortiori,
first order modal logic is interpretable in ZF(C).  In particular the
usual presentation of Gödel's ontological argument is a finite
derivation in first order S5 with the five axioms

* $P(x)\to \Box P(x)$ for positive $P$,
* $P(x)\to P$ is positive,
* $P(x)\land Q(x)\to P(x)$ is positive,
* $\neg P(x)\to P(x)$ is negative,
* $\exists x\,P(x)$ is positive

and the definition

$\displaystyle G(x)\equiv \forall P\,[\,P(x)\to \Box\forall y\,(P(y)\to y=x)\,]$

together with the usual S5 axioms $ \Box A\to A$, $\Box A\to\Box\Box A$
and $\Diamond A\to\Box\Diamond A$.  On that basis one obtains formally

$\vdash \Diamond\exists x\,G(x)$ and, by the axioms above,
$\vdash \exists x\,G(x)$.

So in the same classical meta-theory in which the spectral theorem for
self-adjoint operators on a complex Hilbert space is proved you can
code the modal language of Gödel's argument as a first order theory
and you get a straightforward model-theoretic existence result:
any model of the five positivity axioms and S5 contains an object
which is essentially God-like in Gödel's sense.  That is the only
“existence’’ that the derivation ever gives you: the existence of a
formal model satisfying the stipulated axioms.

It is not an existence proof about the physical world.  It is
conditional on the acceptability of the metaphysical axioms on
positivity, essentialism and the S5 conception of necessity, and it
gives no construction of a physical entity.  In operational terms the
propositions about a quantum system are not the classical Boolean
algebra of subsets of a set but the orthomodular lattice of closed
subspaces / projection operators.  The distributivity and the classical
law of excluded middle which are used essentially in the usual
presentation of the S5 derivation fail for that quantum-logical
propositional structure.  Hence there is no non-trivial proof of the
existence of a real, i.e. physically instantiated, Gödel God-like
entity from the operational content of quantum mechanics; the formal
derivation is just a theorem of the classical mathematics that the
formalism of QM is written in.

8.text:
In the usual presentation of non-relativistic quantum mechanics you work in
ordinary classical mathematics. Formally that is ZFC + analysis, i.e. the
theory of separable complex Hilbert spaces ${\cal H}$, self-adjoint
operators $A=A^{*}$ on ${\cal H}$ and the spectral theorem, the usual
$L^{2}$ theory etc.  It is first order mathematics with the usual
Principle of the Excluded Middle and classical logic.

Gödel's ontological argument is a theorem of modal predicate logic.
In the form usually quoted it is a theorem of S5 with the one non-logical
axioms

* $P$ is positive $\to$ $\Diamond \exists x\,P x$,
* $P$ positive $\to$ $P$ is necessarily positive,
* $P\land Q$ positive if $P$ and $Q$ positive, etc.,

and with the definition

* $G x := \forall P\,[P x \to \Diamond\forall y\, P y]$,
* $E$ is essentially existent: $\Diamond\exists x\,G x$,
* A being is God-like iff $G x$.

From those axioms plus the S5 modal principles one gets
$\exists x\,Gx$ and indeed $\Box\exists x\,Gx$, i.e. the existence of a
necessarily existent maximally positive being.  The argument is formally
correct in S5.  What it does not give you is a proof of the positivity
axioms themselves, and in particular it does not give you a proof of the
existence of a metaphysical necessary being from the facts of physics.

The positivity axioms are not mathematical statements about Hilbert
spaces, operators, spectra, transition probabilities etc.  They are
metaphysical/ conceptual constraints on the notion of a ‘positive
property’.  The customary mathematical language of quantum mechanics
contains no predicate ‘positive property’, no modal operator $\Box$
interpreted as metaphysical necessity, and no way to express
‘necessarily existent’.  The Hilbert-space formalism can certainly be
used as a meta-language in which the S5 proof can be formalised, in the
same way that any first-order theory can be formalised in ZFC, but the
formalisation is just a representation of the argument.  The premises
$P$ positive $\to\Diamond\exists x\,P x$ etc. remain extra-mathematical
postulates and are not theorems of functional analysis, spectral theory
or the usual $C^{*}$–algebraic formulation of quantum mechanics.

Hence the existence of a Gödelian God-like, i.e. a necessarily existent
maximally positive, being is not a theorem of the mathematics that is
customarily used in quantum mechanics.  At best you can say that, once
the modal-ontological axioms are assumed, the argument can be carried
out inside the set-theoretic meta-theory in which quantum mechanics is
normally formulated.  The existence claim is therefore not proved by,
and is not provable from, the physics mathematics alone. ∎

4.text:
In the physics literature the `customary setting’ for non-relativistic
quantum mechanics is a separable complex pre-Hilbert space
${\cal H}$, a *-algebra of observables represented as essentially
self-adjoint operators on ${\cal H}$ and the associated spectral
measure / state space.  Up to the usual identification this is
ordinary real and complex analysis, linear algebra and functional
analysis formalised in ZF C + the usual analysis.  In particular the
formal language of the theory is the first-order language of
complex vector spaces with an inner product and, at most, the usual
measure-theoretic quantifiers.

Gödel’s ontological argument is a derivation in a quantified modal
logic, normally S5, with a second order predicate $P(x)$ for
“positive property” and the two metaphysical axioms

* $P(x)\rightarrow P({\rm Ess}\,x)$,
* $\exists x\,P(x)$ and Necessity of positive properties,

together with the definiens

* $G(x)\equiv \forall P\bigl[P(x)\rightarrow \Box\exists y\,P(y)\bigr]$.

The whole derivation is a statement about essence, positive
properties and metaphysical necessity, i.e. about a modal-ontological
vocabulary.  It is not a statement about vectors, inner products,
self-adjoint operators, spectra or expectation values.  The Hilbert
space formalism of quantum mechanics contains no primitive modal
operator $\square$, no predicate for “essential property” and no
ontological notion of “positive property”.  In the ordinary physical
use of the mathematics one simply has no way to express, let alone
justify, the premises of the Gödel ontological argument.

What can be done is what can always be done for any formal proof.
ZFC, and hence the metamathematics in which the Hilbert-space theory
is usually formalised, is strong enough to formalise first order modal
logic S5 and therefore to translate Gödel’s derivation into a
derivation in the background set theory.  In that purely formal,
meta-mathematical sense the argument can be reproduced inside the
mathematics that underlies quantum theory, and its conclusion is
conditionally true once the unproved modal-ontological axioms about
positivity and essence are granted.  That is a statement about a
formal system, not a statement proved by, or about, the physics of
quantum mechanics.  In the usual physical sense the mathematics of
quantum mechanics is silent on the existence of a Gödelian necessary
being, and no physical proof of a god-like entity can be obtained
from the Hilbert-space formalism itself.

6.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: No, not as a theorem of the Hilbert-space / C*-algebra formalism
that is the customary mathematics of non-relativistic QM.

Gödel’s ontological argument is a theorem of classical higher order modal
logic S5 with a positivity predicate P, Pos and the axiom Necessarily
Pos(P) → Pos(P) and the usual axioms

* P is positive iff necessarily P is positive,
* if P is positive and P → Q then Q is positive,
* etc.

and the modal principle ◊∃x G(x) → ∃x ◊G(x) etc.  In particular the
proof is a proof in a Boolean, classical, two-valued modal logic. The
propositional calculus of the usual QM formalism is not classical.
The propositions of a quantum system are the closed subspaces, resp.
the projection operators, of a complex Hilbert space H, and their
logical structure is the orthomodular lattice L(H) of projections.
L(H) is not distributive and in infinite dimension it is not Boolean.
Hence the Boolean modal algebra required for the Gödel–S5 positivity
apparatus has no faithful non-trivial interpretation in L(H) itself.
In particular the modal operators “necessarily” and “possibly” cannot be
identified with the Born probabilities or with adjointability in a way
that validates the S5 axioms and the classical closure properties of Pos
used in Gödel’s proof.

What you can do is what you can always do: formalise the Gödel
ontological argument in the classical meta-theory in which Hilbert
spaces live, i.e. in ZFC + classical higher order modal logic. In that
meta-theory the argument is a formal derivation, subject to the usual
philosophical objections to the axioms of positivity and to the
S5 necessity. It is not a derivation internal to the linear-algebraic/
quantum-logical language of observables, states and projections. Inside
the customary QM mathematics there is no natural positivity predicate,
no Boolean modal frame and no maximal positive element that can be
identified with Gödel’s God. Hence the existence of a Gödelian god-like
entity is not provable in the QM formalism stricto sensu; at best it
can be reproduced in the classical set-theoretic meta-theory used to
talk about Hilbert spaces.

any model of the five positivity axioms and S5 contains an object
which is essentially God-like in Gödel's sense.  That is the only
“existence’’ that the derivation ever gives you: the existence of a
formal model satisfying the stipulated axioms.

It is not an existence proof about the physical world.  It is
conditional on the acceptability of the metaphysical axioms on
positivity, essentialism and the S5 conception of necessity, and it
gives no construction of a physical entity.  In operational terms the
propositions about a quantum system are not the classical Boolean
algebra of subsets of a set but the orthomodular lattice of closed
subspaces / projection operators.  The distributivity and the classical
law of excluded middle which are used essentially in the usual
presentation of the S5 derivation fail for that quantum-logical
propositional structure.  Hence there is no non-trivial proof of the
existence of a real, i.e. physically instantiated, Gödel God-like
entity from the operational content of quantum mechanics; the formal
derivation is just a theorem of the classical mathematics that the
formalism of QM is written in.

In the usual presentation of non-relativistic quantum mechanics you work in
ordinary classical mathematics. Formally that is ZFC + analysis, i.e. the
theory of separable complex Hilbert spaces ${\cal H}$, self-adjoint
operators $A=A^{*}$ on ${\cal H}$ and the spectral theorem, the usual
$L^{2}$ theory etc.  It is first order mathematics with the usual
Principle of the Excluded Middle and classical logic.

Gödel's ontological argument is a theorem of modal predicate logic.
In the form usually quoted it is a theorem of S5 with the one non-logical
axioms

* $P$ is positive $\to$ $\Diamond \exists x\,P x$,
* $P$ positive $\to$ $P$ is necessarily positive,
* $P\land Q$ positive if $P$ and $Q$ positive, etc.,

and with the definition

* $G x := \forall P\,[P x \to \Diamond\forall y\, P y]$,
* $E$ is essentially existent: $\Diamond\exists x\,G x$,
* A being is God-like iff $G x$.

From those axioms plus the S5 modal principles one gets
$\exists x\,Gx$ and indeed $\Box\exists x\,Gx$, i.e. the existence of a
necessarily existent maximally positive being.  The argument is formally
correct in S5.  What it does not give you is a proof of the positivity
axioms themselves, and in particular it does not give you a proof of the
existence of a metaphysical necessary being from the facts of physics.

The positivity axioms are not mathematical statements about Hilbert
spaces, operators, spectra, transition probabilities etc.  They are
metaphysical/ conceptual constraints on the notion of a ‘positive
property’.  The customary mathematical language of quantum mechanics
contains no predicate ‘positive property’, no modal operator $\Box$
interpreted as metaphysical necessity, and no way to express
‘necessarily existent’.  The Hilbert-space formalism can certainly be
used as a meta-language in which the S5 proof can be formalised, in the
same way that any first-order theory can be formalised in ZFC, but the
formalisation is just a representation of the argument.  The premises
$P$ positive $\to\Diamond\exists x\,P x$ etc. remain extra-mathematical
postulates and are not theorems of functional analysis, spectral theory
or the usual $C^{*}$–algebraic formulation of quantum mechanics.

Hence the existence of a Gödelian God-like, i.e. a necessarily existent
maximally positive, being is not a theorem of the mathematics that is
customarily used in quantum mechanics.  At best you can say that, once
the modal-ontological axioms are assumed, the argument can be carried
out inside the set-theoretic meta-theory in which quantum mechanics is
normally formulated.  The existence claim is therefore not proved by,
and is not provable from, the physics mathematics alone. ∎

In the physics literature the `customary setting’ for non-relativistic
quantum mechanics is a separable complex pre-Hilbert space
${\cal H}$, a *-algebra of observables represented as essentially
self-adjoint operators on ${\cal H}$ and the associated spectral
measure / state space.  Up to the usual identification this is
ordinary real and complex analysis, linear algebra and functional
analysis formalised in ZF C + the usual analysis.  In particular the
formal language of the theory is the first-order language of
complex vector spaces with an inner product and, at most, the usual
measure-theoretic quantifiers.

Gödel’s ontological argument is a derivation in a quantified modal
logic, normally S5, with a second order predicate $P(x)$ for
“positive property” and the two metaphysical axioms

* $P(x)\rightarrow P({\rm Ess}\,x)$,
* $\exists x\,P(x)$ and Necessity of positive properties,

together with the definiens

* $G(x)\equiv \forall P\bigl[P(x)\rightarrow \Box\exists y\,P(y)\bigr]$.

The whole derivation is a statement about essence, positive
properties and metaphysical necessity, i.e. about a modal-ontological
vocabulary.  It is not a statement about vectors, inner products,
self-adjoint operators, spectra or expectation values.  The Hilbert
space formalism of quantum mechanics contains no primitive modal
operator $\square$, no predicate for “essential property” and no
ontological notion of “positive property”.  In the ordinary physical
use of the mathematics one simply has no way to express, let alone
justify, the premises of the Gödel ontological argument.

What can be done is what can always be done for any formal proof.
ZFC, and hence the metamathematics in which the Hilbert-space theory
is usually formalised, is strong enough to formalise first order modal
logic S5 and therefore to translate Gödel’s derivation into a
derivation in the background set theory.  In that purely formal,
meta-mathematical sense the argument can be reproduced inside the
mathematics that underlies quantum theory, and its conclusion is
conditionally true once the unproved modal-ontological axioms about
positivity and essence are granted.  That is a statement about a
formal system, not a statement proved by, or about, the physics of
quantum mechanics.  In the usual physical sense the mathematics of
quantum mechanics is silent on the existence of a Gödelian necessary
being, and no physical proof of a god-like entity can be obtained
from the Hilbert-space formalism itself.

No, not as a theorem of the Hilbert-space / C*-algebra formalism
that is the customary mathematics of non-relativistic QM.

Gödel’s ontological argument is a theorem of classical higher order modal
logic S5 with a positivity predicate P, Pos and the axiom Necessarily
Pos(P) → Pos(P) and the usual axioms

* P is positive iff necessarily P is positive,
* if P is positive and P → Q then Q is positive,
* etc.

and the modal principle ◊∃x G(x) → ∃x ◊G(x) etc.  In particular the
proof is a proof in a Boolean, classical, two-valued modal logic. The
propositional calculus of the usual QM formalism is not classical.
The propositions of a quantum system are the closed subspaces, resp.
the projection operators, of a complex Hilbert space H, and their
logical structure is the orthomodular lattice L(H) of projections.
L(H) is not distributive and in infinite dimension it is not Boolean.
Hence the Boolean modal algebra required for the Gödel–S5 positivity
apparatus has no faithful non-trivial interpretation in L(H) itself.
In particular the modal operators “necessarily” and “possibly” cannot be
identified with the Born probabilities or with adjointability in a way
that validates the S5 axioms and the classical closure properties of Pos
used in Gödel’s proof.

What you can do is what you can always do: formalise the Gödel
ontological argument in the classical meta-theory in which Hilbert
spaces live, i.e. in ZFC + classical higher order modal logic. In that
meta-theory the argument is a formal derivation, subject to the usual
philosophical objections to the axioms of positivity and to the
S5 necessity. It is not a derivation internal to the linear-algebraic/
quantum-logical language of observables, states and projections. Inside
the customary QM mathematics there is no natural positivity predicate,
no Boolean modal frame and no maximal positive element that can be
identified with Gödel’s God. Hence the existence of a Gödelian god-like
entity is not provable in the QM formalism stricto sensu; at best it
can be reproduced in the classical set-theoretic meta-theory used to
talk about Hilbert spaces.

The customary mathematics in which non-relativistic QM is written is
classical.  It is ZFC + analysis, the theory of separable complex
Hilbert spaces ${\cal H}$, self-adjoint operators $A=A^{*}$,
spectral measures, $C^{*}$-algebras, etc.  The language is first order
classical with Boolean logic and excluded middle.

Gödel’s ontological argument is a quantified modal derivation in S5
with a non-logical unary predicate $P(x)$ ‘$x$ has a positive property’,
with

* $P(x)\to\Box P(x)$,
* closure of $P$ under entailment, conjunction, etc.,
* $ {\rm Necessarily\;Existential}$ is positive,
* $G(x)\equiv \forall P\,[P(x)\to\Box P(x)]$  – or the usual essentially
positive variants – is positive,

and the S5 principles $\Box A\to A$, $\Box A\to\Box\Box A$,
$\Diamond A\to\Box\Diamond A$.  With those premises one gets
$\vdash\Box\exists x\,G(x)$ and hence $\vdash\exists x\,G(x)$ in S5.

First order modal logic S5 is interpretable in ZFC, and ZFC is the
meta-theory in which the Hilbert-space formalism is normally formalised.
Hence the derivation can be coded syntactically in the same classical
set-theoretic background that underlies the spectral theorem, the Born
rule, etc.  In that purely syntactic sense the ontological argument is
formalizable in the mathematics used for QM.

What it is not is a theorem of the physical mathematics of QM.
The Hilbert-space/operator-algebra language contains no modal operator
$\Box/\Diamond$, no predicate ‘positive property’, no notion of
essentiality or metaphysical necessity, and no axioms linking positivity
to existence.  The positivity axioms, the S5 conception of necessity and
the essentialist definition of $G$ are substantive metaphysical
postulates, independent of the axioms of a complex Hilbert space,
self-adjointness, spectral measures and the Born rule.

On the operational reading of the QM formalism the claim is even
stronger.  The propositional structure of QM is the orthomodular lattice
$L({\cal H})$ of closed subspaces / projections, non-distributive and
subject to Kochen–Specker contextuality.  Gödel’s proof uses classical
Boolean distributivity and a global non-contextual bivalent valuation of
all properties simultaneously, in particular a maximal conjunction of
positive properties.  That simultaneous maximal conjunction has no
faithful quantum-logical realisation in $L({\cal H})$.  The distributive
inferences on which the S5 positivity closure rests fail in the
quantum propositional calculus.

Hence the existence of a Gödelian god-like, necessarily existent
maximally positive being is not a consequence of the Hilbert-space
formalism itself.  At best it is a conditional theorem of the classical
meta-theory used to speak about Hilbert spaces, valid only on the
acceptance of Gödel’s modal-metaphysical positivity axioms, and it
ceases to be valid on the quantum-logical reading of properties that is
the natural logic of the customary QM formalism. ∎

mechanics is ordinary classical mathematics.  Formally that is ZFC + real and
complex analysis, i.e. separable complex Hilbert spaces ${\cal H}$,
self-adjoint operators, spectral measures, $C^{*}$-algebras, etc., with first
order classical logic and excluded middle.  That is the background in which
the spectral theorem, the Born rule and the whole operational formalism are
written down.

Gödel’s ontological argument is a derivation in quantified modal logic, in the
usual presentation S5 with a one-place predicate $P(x)$ “$x$ is a positive
property”, the essentialist closure $P(x)\to \Box P(x)$, closure under entailment
and conjunction, the axiom that necessary existence is positive and
$\exists xP(x)$ is positive, and

$G(x)\equiv \forall P\,[\,P(x)\to\Box P(x)\,]$

or an equivalent definiens.  On those axioms S5 proves
$\Diamond\exists x G(x)\to\Box\exists x G(x)$ and hence
$\vdash\Box\exists x G(x)$, i.e. a necessarily existent maximally positive
being.

First order S5 is interpretable in ZFC.  Hence in the purely syntactic,
meta-mathematical sense the Gödel derivation can be coded up as a derivation
in the set-theoretic first order theory in which the Hilbert space formalism
lives.  In that trivial representational sense the proof can be written down
inside the same classical background that is used for QM.

What the background does not supply are the premises.  The Hilbert space
calculus contains no primitive modal operator $\Box$, no predicate
“positive property”, no notion of essence or metaphysical necessity, and no
axiom that necessary existence is positive.  The axioms
$P(x)\to\Box P(x)$, closure of positivity under entailment, etc., are
metaphysical and independent of ZFC and of the axioms of a complex Hilbert
space, the spectral theorem, the Born rule or any empirical content of
quantum mechanics.  They are not consequences of the physical postulates of
QM.

In the operational reading the propositions of QM are the orthomodular lattice
$L({\cal H})$ of closed subspaces/projections.  $L({\cal H})$ is non-distributive
and does not admit a global non-contextual Boolean valuation.  Kochen–Specker
contextuality is precisely the failure of the classical Boolean conjunction
and of the simultaneous definite truth-values needed for the maximal
conjunction of positive properties and for the Boolean modal algebra on which
the S5 positivity apparatus rests.  Hence there is no non-trivial
realisation of the Gödelian maximal being inside the quantum-logical
propositional structure itself.

So the argument is formalizable in the classical meta-language used to state
quantum mechanics, and conditionally on the Gödel S5 positivity axioms it is a
theorem of that meta-theory.  It is not a theorem of, nor is it derivable
from, the physical mathematics of quantum mechanics, and in the genuine
quantum-logical reading it has no physical content.  There is no proof of the
physical existence of a Gödelian god-like entity from the customary QM
formalism alone.

* $P(x)\to\Box P(x)$,

* necessary existence is positive, $\exists x P(x)$ is positive,
* $G(x)\equiv\forall P\,[P(x)\to\Box P(x)]$ is positive,
